title: Owning memory safely
objectives: Use `std::unique_ptr` and RAII so memory frees itself.
Choose between a single owner, shared ownership and plain members.

screens.title: Cleanup at the brace

state.caption: While `trade` runs, `p` lives in its frame

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected cleanup to happen later or not at all, as with a garbage collector. C++ runs the destructor at `trade`'s closing brace.
`p` is a local of `trade`, not of `main`. It ends when `trade` returns, before `done`.
`p` lives until the end of its scope, so `trading` prints while it is still open.

hints.text: When does `p`'s frame disappear?
`p` is a local of `trade`.
`trade` prints `trading`, then reaches `}`: `p`'s destructor prints `close VOD`. Only then does `main` print `done`.

feedback.correct: The destructor runs at the closing brace, every time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the exact line where `p` stops existing.

byKey.never: You expected cleanup later, as with a garbage collector. C++ runs the destructor at `trade`'s `}`.

explain.text: `p` lives in `trade`'s frame. At `trade`'s `}` its destructor runs and prints `close VOD`, then `main` prints `done`. That timing is guaranteed, and it is what the rest of this lesson builds on.

hints.text: Find every `return`. Which ones run before line 10?
Line 10 is the only `delete[]`.
Lines 3 and 9 return before line 10 runs. Line 11 comes after the `delete[]`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each `return` against line 10.

byKey.all: Line 11 runs after the `delete[]` on line 10, so it does not leak.

screens.title: Let a destructor free it
screens.prose: Give the memory an owner whose destructor frees it. That pattern is **RAII**: a constructor acquires the resource and the destructor releases it. `std::vector` works this way.

options.why: The vector is a local. Whatever path leaves the function, its destructor runs and frees the buffer.

Every `return` ends the function's frame.
Each `return` ends `vwap`'s frame, and the vector's destructor frees its heap buffer every time.

screens.title: Hand the Book an owner
screens.prose: `std::unique_ptr<T>` owns one heap object and deletes it in its destructor. `std::make_unique<T>()` creates the object and its owner together. You use it like a pointer: `book->add(x)`.

state.caption: Inside the braces: each node has two owners

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected smart pointers to free everything. When `a` and `b` die, each node still owns the other, so neither count reaches 0.
Neither node can go first: each keeps the other's count at 1.

hints.text: At the inner `}`, `a` and `b` die. What is each node's count then?
Each node is still owned by the other's `other` member.
Both counts drop from 2 to 1, never to 0. No destructor runs: the nodes leak.

feedback.correct: A cycle keeps every count above 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each node's owners after `a` and `b` die.

byKey.both: You expected smart pointers to free everything. Each node still owns the other, so neither count reaches 0.

explain.text: When `a` and `b` die, each count drops to 1: the nodes own each other. No destructor runs, and LeakSanitizer on a desk build reports "64 byte(s) leaked in 2 allocation(s)". Break cycles with one clear owner, or a non-owning `std::weak_ptr` for the back link.

screens.title: The rule of zero
screens.question: What should `Desk`'s destructor do?

options.text: Nothing: write no destructor at all

options.why: The `unique_ptr` deletes the `Pricer` itself. A second `delete` would free it twice, which is undefined.
The vector's own destructor frees its elements. Clearing it first adds nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which member does not already free its own memory?

explain.text: Every member is RAII, so destroying a `Desk` destroys them, and they free their memory. No hand-written destructor, so none to get wrong. Raw `new` belongs inside `make_unique`, not in your classes.

screens.title: Who owns an order
screens.prose: An order book holds live orders. Each order belongs to exactly one book. Strategies keep raw `Order*` pointers to their live orders, so an order must stay at one address while the book grows.
screens.question: Which member should the book use?

options.why: When the vector grows, it moves its elements to a new buffer, and every strategy's `Order*` dangles.
Shared ownership blurs who cancels an order, and every copy updates the count in the hot path.
Nothing owns these orders: every cancel path must remember `delete`, and one miss leaks.

hints.text: Two needs: one owner per order, and a fixed address.
A `unique_ptr` keeps its object at one heap address, wherever the pointer itself moves.
`std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Order>>`: the book is the single owner, and each order stays put when the vector grows.

feedback.correct: One owner, fixed addresses, automatic cleanup.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check ownership and what happens when the vector grows.

byKey.value: A growing vector moves its elements, so raw pointers to them dangle.

explain.text: Each order lives at a fixed heap address owned by one `unique_ptr`, so growing the vector moves only the pointers. Erasing the `unique_ptr` cancels and frees the order. Where nothing points into the data, prefer a plain vector: the `cpp-pricing` binomial pricer keeps its lattice as one `std::vector<double>` member, sized once.

ideas: RAII: an object acquires a resource in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, which runs at every exit from the scope, early returns included.
`std::unique_ptr<T>` is the single owner of one heap object. Create it with `std::make_unique`; it cannot be copied, only moved with `std::move`, which leaves the source null.
`std::shared_ptr` counts owners and frees at zero, but cycles never reach zero and the counting costs time. The rule of zero: build from members that own themselves.

formula.name: Ownership
formula.note: Raw pointers may observe; owners should be RAII types.

summary.trap: Smart pointers do not make leaks impossible: two `shared_ptr`s that own each other are never freed.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: `std::move(a)` hands the double over to `b` and leaves `a` empty, so `a == nullptr` is true, printed as 1.
Moving a `unique_ptr` is allowed; only copying is not.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is left in `a` after the move?

explain.text: The move transfers ownership, so `b` owns 101.5 and `a` is null. Reading `*a` now would be a null dereference: check `if (a)` before using a pointer that may have been moved from.

quiz.question: `auto px = std::make_unique<double[]>(3);` How is the memory freed?

options.text: Automatically with `delete[]` when `px` goes out of scope

options.why: The `unique_ptr<double[]>` does that itself; a manual `delete[]` would free it twice.

options.text: Automatically, but with plain `delete`, so it is a bug
options.why: The `[]` in the type makes the `unique_ptr` use `delete[]`. It indexes too: `px[2]`.

feedback.correct: The array form uses `delete[]` for you.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does the `[]` in the type change?

explain.text: `std::unique_ptr<double[]>` owns an array, supports `px[i]` and frees with `delete[]`. A run set `px[2] = 101.5` and read back `0 101.5`: `make_unique` zeroes the elements. For prices, a `std::vector<double>` is still the usual choice.

quiz.question: What is wrong with this function?

options.text: The `Pricer` is never deleted: a raw `new` with no owner leaks

options.why: `p` is never used after the return. The problem is the heap object it pointed at, which nobody frees.

options.text: Nothing: the memory is freed when `p` goes out of scope
options.why: A raw pointer going out of scope frees nothing. Only an owner such as `unique_ptr` deletes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What happens to the `Pricer` when `p` disappears?

explain.text: `p` dies at the `}`, but a raw pointer's death does nothing to its target. Every call leaks one `Pricer`. `auto p = std::make_unique<Pricer>();` fixes it with no other change.

quiz.question: Why does `book.push_back(o);` fail to compile?

options.why: Vectors of `unique_ptr` are common. They only refuse copies.
The compiler does not track nulls. The error is "call to implicitly-deleted copy constructor".

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `push_back(o)` do with `o`?

explain.text: `push_back(o)` copies its argument, and a `unique_ptr` has no copy. `std::move(o)` moves the order into the vector, which becomes the owner, and leaves `o` null.
